title: Parallel analog quantum simulation in homogeneous quantum gases
authors: Diego Hernández Rajkov, Alberto Terenzi, Marcia Frómeta Fernández, Nicola Grani, Massimo Inguscio, Giulia Del Pace, Giacomo Roati
abstract: Analog quantum simulation offers a powerful way to study strongly correlated quantum systems that are beyond the reach of classical computation. In this context, ultracold atomic gases have been demonstrated to be an exceptionally versatile and well-controlled platform for implementing various quantum Hamiltonians. In this work, we extend this level of control to a multiplexed configuration in which distinct quantum-simulation units are independently controlled and engineered starting from a single atomic cloud. We demonstrate multiplexed operation in two representative settings. First, by shaping box-trap potentials and separately controlling the evaporative cooling trajectories, we prepare subsystems at various temperatures across the superfluid transition of the unitary Fermi gas. Second, we demonstrate parallel quantum simulation of the Josephson Hamiltonian across distinct Josephson-junction quantum simulation units with individually tunable parameters, including local phase control to initialize the dynamics. Our scheme provides a versatile route toward systematic studies of dynamics and transport Hamiltonians in strongly correlated ultracold matter. Moreover, it is readily extendable to a wide range of atomic species, geometries, and dimensionalities.
summary: The research demonstrates an advanced technique to create multiple, independently controllable quantum simulation units (QSUs) using ultracold atomic gases. This multiplexed setup allows researchers to simultaneously study complex phenomena like the superfluid transition and Josephson junction dynamics across an array of junctions. It establishes a powerful tool for investigating transport physics in strongly correlated matter.
main_problem: To study strongly correlated quantum systems, particularly dynamics and transport Hamiltonians, beyond classical computational reach.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated parallel analog quantum simulation in two settings: characterizing the superfluid transition across multiple units and simulating Josephson junctions with independent control over local parameters.
method: They utilized a multiplexed configuration of ultracold atomic gases confined in configurable optical box potentials, allowing for independent manipulation of multiple quantum simulation units (QSUs).
model_or_system: The platform uses homogeneous quantum gases (e.g., Fermi gas) to simulate models like the unitary Fermi gas and Josephson junctions. Control is achieved by shaping optical traps and controlling local cooling/phase.
key_observables: Density, Temperature ($T$), Superfluid fractions, population imbalance ($\Delta z$), and relative phase ($\Delta\phi$) measured via in situ imaging and time-of-flight interference.
important_parameters: Tunneling strength ($E_J$), charging energy ($E_C$), local temperature ($T/T_F$), and barrier height ($V_0/\mu$).
main_assumptions: The process assumes quasi-adiabatic evolution during trap reshaping, and the RF thermometry method supports the assumption of local thermal equilibrium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup using DMDs for confinement, show density distribution verification across multiple units (multiplexing), detail local temperature control via RF spectroscopy, and map out Josephson junction dynamics showing frequency/damping evolution with barrier height.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the multiplexed QSU architecture, then demonstrating independent local control over temperature and superfluidity. Subsequently, it applies this framework to simulate coupled Josephson junctions, analyzing the crossover between weak-link and tunneling regimes.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly versatile, scalable experimental platform for studying non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated quantum matter, directly addressing fundamental questions about transport and phase transitions in mesoscopic arrays.

The atomic gas is con- fined by optically repulsive potentials generated with two DMDs, projected along the vertical (DMDv) and horizontal (DMDh) directions, which also define our imaging axes. A magnetic-field gradient levitates the gas, compensating grav- ity for both hyperfine states. Side panels show the integrated 1D profiles along each axis, black curve correspond to the ideal homogeneous profile.
